title: Tiered residency and latency SLA stress probe
content:
Purpose:
This is a working investigation into how our KV residency management interacts with multi-tiered capacity (reserved vs burstable) and the resulting effects on latency SLAs under stress. Goal: identify simple mitigations that reduce p99 SLA violations during sustained bursts without increasing average cost materially.

High-level hypothesis:
- SLA misses at tail are driven by transient NVMe bandwidth saturation triggered when large amounts of high-reuse keys are evicted and then re-prefetched across many workers during tier transitions or slot reclaim.
- Eviction hysteresis + global pin churn amplify the effect: keys that are cheap to refetch but high-reuse cause repeated spillback waves.
- A small, tier-aware residency budget (pin a tiny fraction per-reservation) + bounded prefetch tokens should reduce tail without major hit to hit-rate.

Experiment matrix (what we ran):
- Hardware: 8x A100-ish GPUs per node, local NVMe RAID (3x 3.84TB), dual-socket CPU.
- Config variants:
  1) baseline: LRU eviction, global pinning disabled, prefetch=on (unbounded), residency_budget=default
  2) hysteresis-guard: LRU + eviction_hysteresis_ms=30000, prefetch tokens=200
  3) tiered-pinning: per-reservation pinned_quota=0.5% of keys, prefetch tokens=50
  4) aggressive-prefetch: prefetch tokens=2000 (stress control)
- Workloads: three synthetic mixes derived from production traces: chat-short (avg seq 80), long-context (avg seq 1024 truncated), multi-tenant-mix (50% short, 40% medium, 10% long; heavy slot churn)
- Stress profile: 10min steady-state at 70% capacity, then 30s 4x burst for 10 minutes repeated, plus a simulated reservation reclaim (move threads between reserved pool and on-demand) every 3 minutes to induce residency churn.

Key metrics captured:
- token throughput (tps), p50/p95/p99 generation latency (ms), KV hit-rate (per-request and per-token), NVMe BW (GB/s), NVMe 95th IOPS, CPU steal, replica-level eviction rate (evictions/s), re-prefetch traffic (MB/s), error rates.

Representative observed numbers (multi-tenant-mix):
- Baseline (burst window): p99 = 1,320 ms (SLA target 900 ms) | KV hit-rate 78% | NVMe BW peak 9.6 GB/s | evictions/s 420
- Hysteresis-guard: p99 = 980 ms | KV hit-rate 76% | NVMe BW peak 6.8 GB/s | evictions/s 210
- Tiered-pinning: p99 = 740 ms | KV hit-rate 70% | NVMe BW peak 5.1 GB/s | evictions/s 95
- Aggressive-prefetch: p99 = 1,800 ms | KV hit-rate 83% | NVMe BW peak 12.1 GB/s | evictions/s 520

Notes on the numbers:
- Tiered-pinning produced the best tail improvement at the cost of ~8% absolute hit-rate loss; paradoxically this reduced re-prefetch bandwidth enough to keep NVMe under ~6GB/s which prevented queueing and long tail latencies.
- Hysteresis helps but only half as effective as tiered-pinning for these churny burst patterns.
- Aggressive prefetch increases hit-rate but dramatically increases NVMe traffic and p99 because we overload NVMe queues and create longer service times for spillback reads.

Trace and log snippets (for reproducibility):
- Example trace event around an SLA miss (simplified):
  [2026-02-25T14:12:32.412Z] request: r12345 start -> allocate slot -> KV lookup miss -> enqueue NVMe read (prefetch batch 256) -> NVMe latency 8.2ms per IO -> stall waiting for KV -> model step delayed 16 tokens -> total gen latency 1500ms -> SLA breach

- Command to replay multi-tenant trace (local harness):
  ./harness/run_replay --trace traces/multi-tenant-2026-02-20.json --concurrency 120 --burst-pattern="10m:70%, 30s:4x" --kv-config=baseline.json

Instrument notes: where to look in logs
- telemetry.kv.evictions/s (per-host), telemetry.kv.reprefetch_bytes/s, telemetry.nvme.queue_depth_percent, telemetry.rpc_latencies.p99.
- correlate times where nvme.queue_depth_percent > 60% and reprefetch_bytes/s spikes: those are the windows with most SLA misses.

Behavioral findings (why we think it's happening):
1) Eviction waves: when reservation rebalancing or slot reclaim happens, many workers release a similar set of keys. Global pin daemon currently does not consider tier semantics so pins get removed and re-inserted in bulk, causing synchronized re-prefetch.
2) Prefetch amplification: unbounded prefetch triggers large batched NVMe reads. Long-context requests prefetch many pages and if many such requests appear simultaneously the NVMe becomes the bottleneck.
3) Tail sensitivity: p99 is more sensitive to NVMe queueing than average hit-rate. Small improvements in NVMe bandwidth headroom yield large tail improvements.

Quick wins & mitigations to try (ranked):
- Implement conservative default prefetch tokens per-worker and add a global backoff when node NVMe queue depth crosses 50%. (low-effort)
- Add tier-aware pin quotas: allow each reservation to reserve a tiny percentage of hotset; this reduces cross-pool eviction waves. (medium)
- Introduce staggered pin expiry (jitter) to avoid synchronized re-prefetch during reclaim events. (low)
- Rate-limit prefetch batch size for long-context requests during cluster-wide bursts. (medium)
- Consider admission prioritization for long-context requests under NVMe pressure (drop or slow-start those). (higher-risk)

Potential regressions / tradeoffs observed: 
- Tiered-pinning increases in-memory footprint and lowers global hit-rate modestly; need cost estimate for reserved fleets.
- Hysteresis increases time items stay pinned after cold shift — could increase memory pressure under steady load. Tune carefully.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Q: What fraction of hotset does 0.5% pinned_per_reservation correspond to in production? Need to map to absolute bytes per-reservation (Marcus to run estimate).
- Q: How does this interact with quantized-weight caching (when model weights share the NVMe path)? Do we see co-located IO contention? (Sofia to test co-located synthetic mix)
- TODO: run longer 6-hour overnight runs with tiered-pinning variant and collect cost delta estimate (Devon).
- TODO: wire a dashboard that overlays NVMe queue depth, prefetch bytes/s, and p99 latency on same timeline for triage.

Proposed rollout plan for safe experiment in prod-like env:
1) Canary on a small reserved fleet: enable tiered-pinning with pin_quota=0.2% and prefetch tokens=50. Observe for 24h.
2) If stable: increase pin_quota to 0.5% in increments.
3) Add auto-backoff: if nvme_queue_depth > 60% for >30s then reduce prefetch tokens by 80% node-wide.

Notes-to-self / heuristics discovered:
- "Small pin, big tail benefit": even tiny reserved quotas drastically reduce synchronized refetch waves.
- Prefetch is a double-edged sword: raises hit-rate but can kill tails via IO saturation.

Attachments / artifacts produced during the run:
- charts/multi-tenant/p99-vs-nvme-queue.png
- runs/2026-02-25/tiered-pinning-run.log
- perf/profiles/reprefetch-flame.svg (shows long NVMe stalls in hot windows)

If you pick this up next: start with validating absolute memory cost of per-reservation quotas (sample calculation code below) and then implement a node-level prefetch backoff (small PR scope).

Sample calculation (quick):
- avg key size (opaque) on disk ~ 1.2KB, hotset estimate = 10M keys -> 12GB hotset. 0.5% quota = 50k keys = 60MB per-reservation pinned footprint (fits on host memory but multiply by #reservations). Need real numbers from prod hotset profiler.

End of notes.
